explanations.explanation: The text says these seven cows were “sickly and thin” (Genesis 41:3). They climb out of the Nile and stand right next to the sleek ones on the bank. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, later calls them “sickly, ugly, and thin” (Genesis 41:19). Seven healthy cows and seven skinny ones, side by side, and nobody's asking for a group photo.

Spots are a fair guess for a cow, friend, but the text never mentions any. It says the second seven were “sickly and thin” (Genesis 41:3). The difference is in how healthy they look next to the well-fed ones. Think more bony than patterned.

Wild is a good guess, but the text never calls these cows wild. They come up from the Nile and stand beside the well-fed cows on the bank, as Genesis 41:3 tells it. The word it uses is “sickly and thin.” Picture seven worn-out cows, not seven stampeding ones.

It goes the other way, friend. Nobody gets scared and nobody runs back into the Nile. The text says the sickly, thin cows “devoured the seven sleek, well-fed cows” (Genesis 41:4). The skinny ones are the ones doing the eating.

That's right. The thin cows aren't the ones running anywhere. Genesis 41:4 says they “devoured the seven sleek, well-fed cows.” Pharaoh, king of Egypt, wakes up right after that, and I'd say that makes sense.

Same move as the cows. Genesis 41:7 says “the thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven plump, ripe ones.” Then Pharaoh, king of Egypt, wakes and realizes it was a dream. Two dreams, one pattern. The skinny ones keep winning.

The east wind does show up, but only to scorch them. The text says the seven thin heads were “thin and scorched by the east wind” (Genesis 41:6). They never break off. They swallow up the seven plump, ripe ones (Genesis 41:7). Wind gets a cameo, and the thin heads get the main role.

No harvest scene here, friend. The dream never gets as far as cutting anything down. It says the thin heads of grain “swallowed up the seven plump, ripe ones” (Genesis 41:7). Then Pharaoh, king of Egypt, wakes up.

The text says it plainly: “In the morning his spirit was troubled” (Genesis 41:8). Pharaoh, king of Egypt, just dreamed about skinny cows eating plump cows and thin grain swallowing plump grain, twice. I'd be rattled too. He doesn't shrug it off. He calls for help.
Joyful would mean Pharaoh, king of Egypt, woke up humming. Genesis 41:8 says “his spirit was troubled.” Cows eating cows will do that to a person. He sends for help right away.

Pharaoh, king of Egypt, did sleep twice that night, so rested is a fair guess. But the text says “In the morning his spirit was troubled” (Genesis 41:8). Two strange dreams don't make for a restful night. He gets up and summons people to explain them.

explanations.answer: All the magicians and wise men of Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's the list. Genesis 41:8 says Pharaoh, king of Egypt, “summoned all the magicians and wise men of Egypt.” He tells them both dreams. That's the whole group, not just one or two of them.

explanations.answer: The captain of the guard and his officers
explanations.explanation: The captain of the guard does show up in this passage, but later and in a different way. The cupbearer says the young Hebrew was a servant of the captain of the guard (Genesis 41:12). Pharaoh, king of Egypt, calls for “all the magicians and wise men of Egypt” (Genesis 41:8). Those are the ones who hear the dreams first.

explanations.answer: All the elders of Pharaoh’s household
explanations.explanation: Elders are a sensible guess, but the text doesn't mention them. Genesis 41:8 says Pharaoh, king of Egypt, summoned “all the magicians and wise men of Egypt.” Those are the ones he tells his dreams to. Nobody else is named.

Not quite, friend. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, tells them his dreams, but the text says “no one could interpret them for him” (Genesis 41:8). That includes all the magicians and wise men. They come up empty.

That's right. Genesis 41:8 says Pharaoh, king of Egypt, “told them his dreams, but no one could interpret them for him.” All those wise people in one room and nobody has an answer. I know that quiet room, I've sat in a few.

Yes, he's the one. Genesis 41:9 says “the chief cupbearer said to Pharaoh, ‘Today I recall my failures.’” The cupbearer is the officer who serves Pharaoh's cup. Then he tells the king about the young Hebrew who once interpreted his dream.

The captain of the guard is in the story, but he isn't the one who speaks up. The cupbearer says he and the chief baker were put in the custody of the captain of the guard (Genesis 41:10). Then “the chief cupbearer said to Pharaoh…” (Genesis 41:9). He's the one with the memory.

The chief baker was the cupbearer's fellow prisoner, so it's a natural guess. But the cupbearer says “the other man was hanged” (Genesis 41:13). The baker isn't the one speaking up. The chief cupbearer does that (Genesis 41:9).

explanations.answer: He was restored to his position
explanations.explanation: He says it himself: “I was restored to my position” (Genesis 41:13). That's exactly what the young Hebrew had told him. The cupbearer is back serving Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He just took two years to say thanks out loud.

explanations.answer: He was sold as a servant
explanations.explanation: That's not what the cupbearer says. He says, “I was restored to my position” (Genesis 41:13). He gets his old job back, not a new owner. It's the good half of the two interpretations.

explanations.answer: He was made captain of the guard
explanations.explanation: The captain of the guard is the man who held the cupbearer in custody (Genesis 41:10). The cupbearer doesn't take his job. Genesis 41:13 says, “I was restored to my position.” He goes back to the work he had before.

That's right. Genesis 41:14 says “Pharaoh sent for Joseph, who was quickly brought out of the dungeon.” Joseph is the young Hebrew the cupbearer told him about. After two years in there, I think that was a very good morning.

It does happen, friend. After the cupbearer speaks, “Pharaoh sent for Joseph, who was quickly brought out of the dungeon” (Genesis 41:14). Joseph is the young Hebrew the cupbearer described. He doesn't stay in there another day.

explanations.answer: He says God will give the answer
explanations.explanation: Joseph answers, “I myself cannot do it, but God will give Pharaoh a sound answer” (Genesis 41:16). Joseph, the young Hebrew, is standing in front of the king of Egypt. He points to God instead of himself. That's a humble answer in a big room.

explanations.answer: He says he has done this before
explanations.explanation: The cupbearer did say Joseph interpreted dreams in custody (Genesis 41:12). But Joseph doesn't brag about it here. He says, “I myself cannot do it, but God will give Pharaoh a sound answer” (Genesis 41:16). He gives God the credit.

explanations.answer: He asks for his freedom first
explanations.explanation: Joseph has been in the dungeon, so I get why that came to mind. But the text doesn't have him ask for anything. He tells Pharaoh, king of Egypt, “I myself cannot do it, but God will give Pharaoh a sound answer” (Genesis 41:16). The answer comes before any request.

Pharaoh, king of Egypt, says the opposite. After devouring the well-fed cows, “no one could tell that they had done so; their appearance was as ugly as it had been before” (Genesis 41:21). The thin cows eat all that and still look the same. If I ate seven cows I'd want to look a little different.

That's right. Pharaoh says that after they devoured the well-fed cows, “no one could tell that they had done so; their appearance was as ugly as it had been before” (Genesis 41:21). It's one of the details he stresses to Joseph, the young Hebrew. Then he says he woke up.

Joseph says just the opposite. He tells Pharaoh, king of Egypt, “The dreams of Pharaoh are one and the same” (Genesis 41:25). A cow dream and a grain dream, but one message. Verse 26 repeats it: “The dreams have the same meaning.”
That's right. Joseph says, “The dreams of Pharaoh are one and the same” (Genesis 41:25). He says it again in verse 26: “The dreams have the same meaning.” Two dreams, one message.

Joseph says, “God has revealed to Pharaoh what He is about to do” (Genesis 41:25). The dreams are about what God is about to do. Joseph, the young Hebrew, said earlier that God would give the answer (Genesis 41:16). He's staying consistent.

The dreams are Pharaoh's, so I see why you picked him. But Joseph says, “God has revealed to Pharaoh what He is about to do” (Genesis 41:25). God is the one who is about to act. Pharaoh is the one being shown.

Egypt is where all of this happens, but Egypt isn't the one acting. Joseph says, “God has revealed to Pharaoh what He is about to do” (Genesis 41:25). Pharaoh, king of Egypt, is shown what God is about to do. The land is where it happens.

That's what Joseph says. The seven thin cows and the seven worthless heads of grain scorched by the east wind “are seven years of famine” (Genesis 41:27). Seven good years, then seven hard ones. Joseph, the young Hebrew, makes the pattern clear.

War is a big guess, but Joseph never says it. He says the thin cows and scorched heads of grain “are seven years of famine” (Genesis 41:27). Nothing about armies in this passage. It's about the land running short.

Plague doesn't appear in Joseph's explanation. He says the thin cows and scorched heads of grain “are seven years of famine” (Genesis 41:27). The same word comes back in verse 30: “the famine will devastate the land.” Famine is the word to hold onto.

It's the other way around, friend. Joseph says, “all the abundance in the land of Egypt will be forgotten” (Genesis 41:30). Then he adds, “The abundance in the land will not be remembered, since the famine that follows it will be so severe” (Genesis 41:31). The hard years will be that heavy.

That's right. Joseph says the abundance “will be forgotten” and “will not be remembered” once the famine arrives (Genesis 41:30-31). He says the famine will be that severe. It's like the good batch you can't remember while the oven's cold.

explanations.answer: God decreed it and will do it shortly
explanations.explanation: Joseph says, “because the dream was given to Pharaoh in two versions, the matter has been decreed by God, and He will carry it out shortly” (Genesis 41:32). The two versions go with God having decreed it. Joseph, the young Hebrew, tells Pharaoh, king of Egypt, this directly.

explanations.answer: So Pharaoh would remember it longer
explanations.explanation: Remembering it longer makes sense, since Pharaoh woke up shaken. But Joseph gives a different reason. He says it was given in two versions because “the matter has been decreed by God, and He will carry it out shortly” (Genesis 41:32). The text doesn't mention Pharaoh's memory.

explanations.answer: Because the magicians missed the first one
explanations.explanation: The magicians did miss it, since “no one could interpret them” (Genesis 41:8). But the second dream came during the same night, before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, ever told anyone. Joseph says it was given in two versions because “the matter has been decreed by God, and He will carry it out shortly” (Genesis 41:32).

Joseph says, “Pharaoh should look for a discerning and wise man and set him over the land of Egypt” (Genesis 41:33). After laying out the dream, Joseph, the young Hebrew, moves on to what to do about it. This man is going to have a big job.

A soldier sounds good for a big job. But Joseph never mentions one. He tells Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to look for “a discerning and wise man” (Genesis 41:33). The job calls for good judgment, not muscle.

A merchant would know about trade, so I see the thinking. But Joseph asks for something else. He says Pharaoh, king of Egypt, should look for “a discerning and wise man” and set him over the land (Genesis 41:33). Money isn't on the list.

Joseph says Pharaoh, king of Egypt, should “appoint commissioners over the land to take a fifth of the harvest of Egypt during the seven years of abundance” (Genesis 41:34). One out of every five. Joseph, the young Hebrew, is working out the numbers like he's done it before.

A tenth is a common number, so I see why it came up. But Joseph says commissioners should “take a fifth of the harvest of Egypt during the seven years of abundance” (Genesis 41:34). That's more than a tenth. Twice as much, in fact.

A third would be a bigger share, but that's not Joseph's number. He tells Pharaoh, king of Egypt, that commissioners should “take a fifth of the harvest of Egypt during the seven years of abundance” (Genesis 41:34). One out of five, friend.

explanations.answer: A reserve for the famine years
explanations.explanation: Joseph says, “This food will be a reserve for the land during the seven years of famine to come upon the land of Egypt” (Genesis 41:36). The grain gathered in the good years waits in the cities. Then the lean years arrive and it's already there.

Joseph never mentions a gift for officials. The commissioners do collect the grain “under the authority of Pharaoh” (Genesis 41:35). But he says the food “will be a reserve for the land during the seven years of famine” (Genesis 41:36). It's for the whole land.

explanations.answer: Goods to trade with other nations
explanations.explanation: Trading is a smart business idea, but Joseph doesn't say it here. He says the stored food “will be a reserve for the land during the seven years of famine to come upon the land of Egypt” (Genesis 41:36). The grain is for Egypt's own famine years.

That's what Joseph says. The stored food will be a reserve, “Then the country will not perish in the famine” (Genesis 41:36). He's the young Hebrew who stood in front of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and gave him both the warning and a plan. The grain is the difference.

Joseph says it will work, friend. He tells Pharaoh, king of Egypt, “Then the country will not perish in the famine” (Genesis 41:36). That's the point of storing the food. The plan comes with a promise.
